title: Ζεὺς κριτής
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 126 (= Perry 313). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὁ Ζεὺς τὰς τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἁμαρτίας ἐν ὀστράκοις τὸν Ἑρμῆν ὥρισε γράφειν, καὶ εἰς κιβώτιον ἀποτιθέναι πλησίον αὐτοῦ, ὅπως ἑκάστου τὰς δίκας ἀναπράσσῃ.
sentences.tr: Ho Zeus tas tōn anthrōpōn hamartias en ostrakois ton Hermēn hōrise graphein, kai eis kibōtion apotithenai plēsion autou, hopōs hekastou tas dikas anaprassēi.
sentences.l: Zeus appointed Hermes to write men's faults upon potsherds, and to lay them away in a box near himself, so that he might exact from each man his penalties.
sentences.n: ὁρίζω is to set a boundary, hence to lay a thing down as fixed; with the accusative and infinitive it is 'he laid it down that Hermes should write'. Potsherds were the cheapest writing material there was: the shards of a broken jar were good for nothing else, but served for a note, and for the ballot of ostracism. ἀναπράσσω is the collector's word, to exact a payment that is owed, and δίκη in the plural is the penalty itself rather than the trial.

sentences.t: Συγκεχυμένων δὲ τῶν ὀστράκων ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοις, τὸ μὲν βράδιον, τὸ δὲ τάχιον ἐμπίπτει εἰς τὰς τοῦ Διὸς χεῖρας, εἴποτε καλῶς κρίνοιτο.
sentences.tr: Synkechymenōn de tōn ostrakōn ep’ allēlois, to men bradion, to de tachion empiptei eis tas tou Dios cheiras, eipote kalōs krinoito.
sentences.l: But the potsherds having been poured together one upon another, one falls more slowly, another more quickly, into the hands of Zeus, if ever it should be rightly judged.
sentences.n: Genitive absolute again: the noun and its participle stand outside the sentence's own construction and give the circumstance — 'the potsherds having been poured together'. βράδιον and τάχιον are comparative adverbs measured against each other, as the μέν…δέ shows: one sherd comes up sooner than the next. εἴποτε with the optative is the indefinite 'if ever'; what κρίνοιτο takes as its subject is left unsaid — the sherd, or the case written on it — and the Greek does not settle it.

sentences.t: Ὅτι οὐ χρὴ θαυμάζειν διὰ τοὺς ἀδίκους καὶ πονηροὺς ὅτι τάχιον οὐκ ἀπολαμβάνουσιν ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀδικιῶν αὐτῶν.
sentences.tr: Hoti ou chrē thaumazein dia tous adikous kai ponērous hoti tachion ouk apolambanousin hyper tōn adikiōn autōn.
sentences.l: That one must not wonder, on account of the unjust and the wicked, that they do not the sooner receive their due for their wrongdoings.
sentences.i: The story shows that one must not wonder, on account of the unjust and the wicked, that they do not the sooner receive their due for their wrongdoings.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. The second ὅτι is an ordinary one, giving the content of the wondering. ἀπολαμβάνω is to take back what belongs to one, here of a debt falling due; ὑπέρ with the genitive is 'in return for'.
